items.answer: Immersion is the objective, quantifiable degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in an extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing way.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Three-dimensional registration is the anchoring of virtual content in augmented reality at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.

Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

questions.question: In virtual reality, what does a high degree of presence give a user?
options: Belief that the real world is the virtual world
Belief that the virtual world is an artificial display
Belief that the virtual world is the real world
Belief that the real world is an augmented overlay
questions.explanation: Presence means the user believes they are in the real world while actually in a virtual world. The other options reverse the relationship or describe non-presence states.

questions.question: What two virtual-reality goals follow from different conceptions of reality?
options: match real-world overlays closely, or surpass them
match real-world actions closely, or surpass them
match real-world experiences closely, or surpass them
match real-world visuals closely, or surpass them
questions.explanation: Different conceptions of reality yield two goals: matching real-world experience closely, or surpassing lived day-to-day reality. Actions, visuals, and overlays are design or interaction concerns, not the conceptions of reality named here.

questions.question: Why can one virtual reality system be considered good by some users and bad by others?
options: A system that satisfies one level of immersion may not satisfy another, and a system that exceeds comfort may feel dizzying or hard to understand
A system that satisfies one amount of detail may not satisfy another, and a system that exceeds realistic graphics may feel noisy or hard to understand
A system that satisfies one style of control may not satisfy another, and a system that exceeds familiar actions may feel clumsy or hard to understand
A system that satisfies one notion of reality may not satisfy another, and a system that exceeds reality may feel eerie or hard to understand
questions.explanation: Different users hold different conceptions of reality, so a system that matches one group's standard may not be seen as good by another, and a system that goes beyond reality can feel creepy or difficult to comprehend. The wrong options substitute comfort, control, or graphics for the issue of reality.

data.text: VR systems aim for presence, the feeling that a virtual world is experienced as real. People differ in what counts as reality: some expect virtual reality to match real-world perception and sensation, while others expect it to go beyond everyday reality. This difference makes judging presence ambiguous, because a system that works for one group may not work for another.
points: A VR system aims for presence, making users believe the virtual world is real; closer to that goal, immersion improves.
Some people treat real-world perception and sensation as the gold standard, so virtual reality should match them closely.
For others, virtual reality should surpass everyday lived reality rather than imitate it exactly.
Different conceptions of reality make virtual reality evaluation ambiguous, because matching or surpassing reality may not satisfy all users.

questions.question: What makes an almost-real virtual human feel uncanny?
options: Gross distortions that are readily recognizable at first
Low human likeness that is readily recognizable at first
Subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first
Minor human imperfections that are readily recognizable at first
questions.explanation: The uncanny valley effect is triggered when a virtual human is close enough to real to seem familiar, but small flaws make it feel off. Clearly artificial, low-likeness, or obviously flawed figures are not the described cause.

questions.question: In the uncanny valley pattern, what happens to familiarity as human likeness increases?
options: It first decreases, then increases, and then decreases afterward
It first decreases, then increases, and then stays high afterward
It first increases, then decreases, and then increases afterward
It first increases, then decreases, and then stays low afterward
questions.explanation: Familiarity rises as a virtual object becomes more human-like, drops in the uncanny valley region, and rises again after that region. A pattern that stays low or high after the valley does not match the described curve.

questions.question: What design trade-off does the uncanny valley effect create for a VR designer?
options: The exact match with real-world appearance in a human-like figure
The amount of realism to include in a human-like figure
The avoidance of human-like features in a human-like figure
The maximum realism achievable in a human-like figure
questions.explanation: The effect means that matching reality exactly can backfire, so the designer has a trade-off over how much realism to include. It does not require exact realism, maximum realism, or avoidance of human likeness.

data.text: The uncanny valley effect shows that increasing human likeness does not continuously increase familiarity. It describes how almost-real digital humans can feel eerie because of subtle imperfections, with a sharp dip in familiarity in 70-85% human likeness, especially for moving objects. In VR, this makes exact realism a design risk, so the amount of realism must be chosen as a trade-off.
points: The uncanny valley effect is that almost-real digital humans can feel eerie because of subtle imperfections.
The uncanny valley plot shows familiarity rising, falling sharply in 70-85% human likeness, especially for moving objects, then rising again.
In VR, near-real human-like figures can be unpleasant, so creators must choose how much realism to include.

activities.title: Order the changes in familiarity as human likeness increases in the uncanny valley

items.title: Order the changes in familiarity as human likeness increases in the uncanny valley
steps: Familiarity increases for both moving and stationary objects
Familiarity decreases, more sharply for moving objects
Familiarity reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley region
Familiarity increases for digital objects at high human likeness

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares photorealism with other cues for VR presence?
options: Photorealism is not required, while other cues can be useful
Photorealism is required, while other cues are not useful
Photorealism is required, while other cues can be useful
Photorealism is not required, while other cues are not useful
questions.explanation: Presence does not depend on photorealism, and other cues may be useful. The other options wrongly add a requirement for photorealism or wrongly deny the usefulness of other cues.

questions.question: Which statement best describes representational fidelity in a VR experience?
options: How closely the user's physical movements match an equivalent real-world task
How familiar the virtual place is, or could be, in real-world experience
How closely the user's experience matches the creator's intended experience
How strongly the environment uses photorealistic 360-degree views of real places
questions.explanation: Representational fidelity concerns familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth. The other options describe interaction fidelity, experiential fidelity, or a strong indicator rather than the underlying measure.

questions.question: Which user behavior indicates high interaction fidelity?
options: Watching photorealistic 360-degree images
Seeing almost human-like figures
Pressing buttons with no body motion
Performing realistic physical actions
questions.explanation: High interaction fidelity uses realistic physical actions for virtual tasks. Button-press movement with no body motion is very low interaction fidelity, while photorealistic images and human-like figures concern representation or the uncanny valley.

questions.question: What change to a free-roaming VR world is associated with higher experiential fidelity?
options: Using photorealistic real-world views
Adding real-world constraints
Making figures almost human-like
Removing real-world constraints
questions.explanation: Higher experiential fidelity comes from real-world constraints on virtual navigation, movement, and interaction. Removing constraints leaves each user with a different unbounded experience, while photorealism and human-like figures address other concerns.

data.text: VR presence is not achieved only by making virtual objects photorealistic or human-like, because familiar cues in the virtual environment can support it. Representational, interaction, and experiential fidelity are the main design axes, each moving toward higher fidelity when virtual places, user actions, and personal experiences more closely match real-world or intended conditions. Maintaining all three fidelities as highly as possible helps keep the uncanny valley from disrupting the virtual experience.
points: Presence in VR does not require photorealism or human-like objects; developers should balance representational, interaction, and experiential fidelity.
Representational fidelity is how much a VR place conveys familiarity with an Earthly place, from photorealistic views to abstract worlds.
Interaction fidelity is how well virtual task actions correspond to real-world physical actions, from realistic motion to buttons.
Experiential fidelity is how closely the user's experience matches the creator's intended experience, with real-world constraints raising it.
VR developers should limit the uncanny valley by maintaining all three fidelities as high as possible.

questions.question: Why are AR challenges usually treated as mainly technological rather than psychological?
options: Because AR removes the real environment, psychological effects are harder to control than in VR
Because AR presents fully synthetic objects, immersion demands are higher than in VR
Because immersion is less central in AR, psychological effects are less important than in VR
Because AR combines real and virtual content, psychological effects are stronger than in VR
questions.explanation: AR is not as immersive as VR because it keeps the real world in view, so its main difficulties are technological. Options that describe AR as removing or fully replacing the real world misstate AR.

questions.question: What does suitable display technology need to do in AR?
options: Hide the physical surroundings from the user's view of the real world
Generate a fully synthetic environment instead of the real world
Overlay virtual content on the device's representation of the real world
Update the viewer's pose relative to an anchor in the real world
questions.explanation: AR display technology must let virtual content appear on top of the real-world view. Hiding the real world or generating a fully synthetic environment describes VR, and pose updating is a tracking function, not a display function.

questions.question: What do input devices and modalities primarily enable in AR?
options: Updating of the viewer's pose relative to an anchor in the real world
Interaction with digital content overlaid on the real world
Anchoring of virtual content in a suitable place in the real world
Display of virtual content overlaid on the real world
questions.explanation: Input devices and modalities are the means by which the user interacts with AR content. Displaying, anchoring, and pose updating are separate functions.

questions.question: What does 3D registration mean in AR?
options: Anchoring virtual content at a suitable place in the real world
Replacing the physical scene with a virtual representation of the real world
Displaying virtual content on a screen without linking it to the real world
Updating the viewer's pose relative to an anchor in the real world
questions.explanation: 3D registration anchors virtual objects in real-world locations so they mix seamlessly with physical objects. Replacing the scene is VR-like, unlinked display is not registration, and pose updating is tracking.

questions.question: How do the registration and tracking phases differ in AR pose determination?
options: Registration determines the initial pose relative to an anchor, and tracking updates it as the viewer moves
Registration hides the physical scene from the user, and tracking reveals it as the viewer moves
Registration anchors virtual content in the real world, and tracking displays it as the viewer moves
Tracking determines the initial pose relative to an anchor, and registration updates it as the viewer moves
questions.explanation: In pose determination, registration establishes the viewer's starting pose relative to a real-world anchor, while tracking keeps updating that pose as movement occurs. The reversed option confuses the roles of the two phases.

data.text: Using Azuma's 1997 definition of augmented reality, the main AR challenges are technological rather than psychological. They concern display and interaction: suitable display technology must overlay virtual content on the real-world representation, and suitable input modalities must support real-time interaction. A third challenge is 3D registration, in which virtual content is anchored to the real world by determining the viewer's pose and updating it through registration and tracking.
points: Augmented reality challenges are mostly technological rather than psychological because immersion is less important than in virtual reality.
Azuma's 1997 definition of augmented reality is used to identify its main technological challenges.
Augmented reality display challenges involve overlaying virtual content on the device's real-world view, similar to virtual reality.
Augmented reality interaction requires suitable input devices and modalities for real-time interaction with overlaid digital content.
Augmented reality 3D registration anchors virtual content by determining the viewer's pose; registration sets it and tracking updates it.

questions.question: Which kind of concern is tied to presence in virtual reality?
options: An input-mechanism concern
A technological concern
A psychological concern
A display-technology concern
questions.explanation: Presence is tied to psychological issues in VR, while immersion is tied to technological issues. Display and input mechanisms are technological issues, not the concern tied to presence.

questions.question: In virtual reality, which description matches the uncanny valley effect?
options: A sense of disorientation caused by a virtual environment made unfamiliar to real-world experience
A sense of discomfort caused by a virtual environment made inconsistent with real-world experience
A sense of distrust caused by a virtual environment made abstract to real-world experience
A sense of uneasiness caused by a virtual environment made familiar to real-world experience
questions.explanation: The uncanny valley effect is uneasiness or creepiness that can appear when a virtual environment is made too familiar to the user's real-world experience, not merely when it is unfamiliar, abstract, or inconsistent.

questions.question: What makes the major issues in augmented reality mostly technological?
options: They concern display technology, input mechanisms, and pose estimation
They concern head-mounted displays, virtual environments, and immersive gaming
They concern presence, immersion, and the uncanny valley effect
They concern representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity
questions.explanation: AR's major issues are mostly technological because they center on proper display, input mechanisms, and pose estimation/tracking. The other options list VR or general XR concepts rather than the major AR issues.

data.text: Virtual reality and augmented reality face different major issues. In virtual reality, technological and psychological concerns lead to immersion and presence, while environments that are too familiar can cause an uncanny valley, which builders avoid by attending to representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity. In augmented reality, the main problems are mostly technological: display, input mechanisms, and pose tracking.
points: Virtual reality systems have technological and psychological concerns, tied respectively to immersion and presence.
In virtual reality, the uncanny valley effect is unease caused by environments that are too familiar.
Builders avoid the virtual reality uncanny valley by attending to representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity.
Major augmented reality issues are technological: display, input mechanisms, and pose tracking at the start and during use.

options: Display technology
User presence
Input mechanism
Pose estimation
items.reason: Display technology, input mechanism, and pose estimation are the main technological issues in augmented reality, whereas user presence is a psychological concept tied to virtual reality.

questions.question: How does the ambiguity of reality in virtual reality create a design trade-off over realism?
questions.reference_answer: The trade-off arises because some users want virtual reality to match reality, while others want it to surpass their everyday experience. A system that matches one conception may not satisfy another, and almost-real human-like figures can trigger the uncanny valley. Designers must therefore decide how much realism to include.

questions.question: How does the systemic definition of augmented reality point to its three main technological issues?
questions.reference_answer: The definition points to its issues by requiring combining real and virtual content, real-time interaction, and three-dimensional registration. Combining requires display technology to overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world. Interaction requires suitable input devices and modalities. Registration requires pose, where pose means position and orientation; the registration phase determines the initial pose, and the tracking phase updates it as the user moves.

questions.question: How are the registration and tracking phases of pose estimation needed for three-dimensional registration in augmented reality?
questions.reference_answer: Registration and tracking phases are needed because three-dimensional registration must keep virtual content anchored to the real world while the viewer moves. Pose means position and orientation relative to an anchor, and three-dimensional registration requires that pose to be estimated. The registration phase determines the initial pose at start, and the tracking phase updates it as the user moves, so the virtual content remains properly mixed.
